title: Coronavirus Goes Viral: Quantifying the COVID-19 Misinformation Epidemic on Twitter
screen_reason: Content analysis of 673 English-language tweets retrieved on 27 February 2020 with 11 COVID-19 hashtags and 3 key terms. Tweets were coded against WHO, CDC, peer-reviewed journals and prominent news outlets; 153 tweets (24.8%) contained misinformation. That is a CONTENT share of items in a keyword-defined sample judged against an external ground truth.

estimates.country: Not stated; English-language tweets worldwide (authors based in Lebanon)
estimates.measure_type: % of COVID-19-related tweets that contained misinformation
estimates.denominator: COVID-19 tweets remaining after humorous/non-serious posts were excluded, from 673 English-language tweets with at least five retweets sampled (50 at random per search term) across 11 hashtags and 3 key terms
estimates.definition: Tweet included information that could be clearly refuted using WHO, CDC, peer-reviewed scientific journals or prominent news outlets
estimates.misinfo_def: Misinformation can be defined as a "claim of fact that is currently false due to lack of scientific evidence"
estimates.n: about 617 non-humorous tweets (673 tweets collected; the exact post-exclusion denominator is not printed)
estimates.source_quote: In total, after excluding humorous/non-serious posts, 153 tweets (24.8%) included misinformation, and 107 (17.4%) included unverifiable information.
estimates.page_loc: Results, Misinformation and unverifiable information, p. 4
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Authors (medical students and faculty at the American University of Beirut) summarised and assessed each tweet against WHO, CDC, peer-reviewed journals and prominent news outlets; no inter-rater reliability reported and no coding procedure described beyond cross-matching
estimates.moderator_quote: We performed an online search of the Twitter social media platform on February 27, 2020. We used the Twitter Archiver add-on to search Twitter for tweets containing one or more of 11 common hashtags and three common key terms pertaining to the COVID-19 epidemic
estimates.notes: The printed denominator is inconsistent: 153/24.8% implies about 617 tweets, but 673 were collected and 41 were humorous (which would leave 632), and Table 3's subgroup denominators sum to 564. I recorded the value as printed and flagged the denominator ambiguity rather than recomputing. Retweet-threshold plus per-term random-50 sampling makes the corpus curated. Confidence medium because of the denominator inconsistency and the absence of any inter-rater reliability.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) 107 tweets (17.4%) with 'unverifiable information' — by the paper's own definition these could not be proven correct or incorrect, so they are not classified false and do not belong in a prevalence numerator; adding them to the 24.8% would be a cross-category sum barred by R8; (b) 548 (81.4%) genuine content — an absence numerator, the mirror of the misinformation share, on a different (673-tweet) denominator; (c) the account-type and verification subgroup rates (informal 33.8%, business/NGO/government 6.1%, news outlets 18.6%, healthcare 12.3%, unverified 31.0%, verified 12.6%, follower-count splits) — subgroup breakdowns, not the paper's headline figure; (d) the by-hashtag misinformation rates in Figure 2A, which are only shown graphically with no printed values; (e) tone and topic descriptives (91.2% serious, 69.5% medical/public health, etc.), which are not veracity measures.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of a single-day Twitter search (27 February 2020) using the Twitter Archiver add-on over 11 hashtags and 3 key terms identified by Symplur; English only; tweets with four or fewer retweets excluded; where a term returned more than 100 eligible tweets, 50 were drawn by computer-generated random sequence; 673 tweets analysed. Coding done by the authors against WHO, CDC, peer-reviewed journals and news outlets; no inter-rater reliability, no double coding and no codebook reported; chi-square tests for associations.
rob.item6_quote: Tweets that included information that could be clearly refuted using one of the above-mentioned references were considered under misinformation.
rob.item10_quote: In total, after excluding humorous/non-serious posts, 153 tweets (24.8%) included misinformation, and 107 (17.4%) included unverifiable information.
